top_cited_works.title: Laser Rayleigh scattering
top_cited_works.abstract: Rayleigh scattering is a powerful diagnostic tool for the study of gases and is particularly useful for aiding in the understanding of complex flow fields and combustion phenomena. Although the mechanism associated with the scattering, induced electric dipole radiation, is conceptually straightforward, the features of the scattering are complex because of the anisotropy of molecules, collective scattering from many molecules and inelastic scattering associated with rotational and vibrational transitions. These effects cause the scattered signal to be depolarized and to have spectral features that reflect the pressure, temperature and internal energy states of the gas. The very small scattering cross section makes molecular Rayleigh scattering particularly susceptible to background interference. Scattering from very small particles also falls into the Rayleigh range and may dominate the scattering from molecules if the particle density is high. This particle scattering can be used to enhance flow visualization and velocity measurements, or it may be removed by spectral filtering. top_cited_works.title: Optical third-harmonic generation in alkali metal vapors
top_cited_works.abstract: This paper considers third-harmonic generation in phase-matched mixtures of alkali metal vapors and inert gases. Calculations show that the combination of near-resonant nonlinear susceptibilities, the ability to phase match, and the relatively high UV transparency of these vapors should allow high conversion efficiency for picosecond laser pulses with a peak power of 108-109W. Calculations of the nonlinear susceptibility and of the ratio of xenon atoms to metal vapor atoms which is necessary to achieve phase matching are given for each of the alkalies as a function of incident laser wavelength. Processes that limit the allowable peak power density and energy density are discussed and guides for determining the metal vapor pressure, cell length, and beam area are given.

top_cited_works.title: High-Gain Backward Lasing in Air
top_cited_works.abstract: The compelling need for standoff detection of hazardous gases and vapor indicators of explosives has motivated the development of a remotely pumped, high-gain air laser that produces lasing in the backward direction and can sample the air as the beam returns. We demonstrate that high gain can be achieved in the near-infrared region by pumping with a focused ultraviolet laser. The pumping mechanism is simultaneous resonant two-photon dissociation of molecular oxygen and resonant two-photon pumping of the atomic oxygen fragments. The high gain from the millimeter-length focal zone leads to equally strong lasing in the forward and backward directions. Further backward amplification is achieved with the use of earlier laser spark dissociation. Low-divergence backward air lasing provides possibilities for remote detection.

recent_works.title: Effect of Magnetic Field on Laser Absorption in Xe Isotopes at 788 nm
recent_works.abstract: The two-photon absorption of a linearly or circularly polarized UV beam of a femtosecond laser at 256 nm is used to pump ground-state electrons of Xe-129 and Xe-136 to sublevels of the 6p [5/2] 2 excited state depending on the polarization. A copropagating linearly or circularly polarized IR beam of a picosecond laser at near 788.132 nm is used to further excite these electrons to the 8s [3/2]° 2 state through a single photon absorption process. The absorption of the IR beam is measured by a fast detector. The type and handedness of polarization of the two beams result in different absorption of IR in the final transition. The effect of applying an external magnetic field on the absorption of the IR beam is studied.

Numerical Modeling of the Propagation of Shaped Laser Beams Through Aerosols
recent_works.abstract: The propagation of high-power laser beams is strongly affected by absorption-induced thermal blooming, which generates refractive index gradients and degrades beam quality. In this work, a numerical framework is developed to investigate the interaction between shaped laser beams and aerosol-induced thermal fields. The model combines the paraxial wave equation for optical propagation with a coupled fluid solver based on the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Aerosol absorption is modeled using the Mie scattering theory, and the bulk absorption coefficient is obtained by integrating particle-scale absorption efficiencies over a particle size distribution. Three shaped laser beams are examined, such as a Gaussian beam, a shifted Gaussian beam with a ring-like focus, and a first-order Bessel-Gauss beam. Analysis of the normalized beam power as a function of propagation distance demonstrates that shaped beams maintain higher transmitted power and improved beam quality under preheated conditions, and the shifted Gaussian beam shows the best overall performance. recent_works.title: Design and Characterization of a Bench-Top Ludwieg Tube for Aerodynamic Measurements via Simultaneous Quantification of Mach Number and Velocity
recent_works.abstract: This article presents the design and detailed characterization of a new supersonic wind tunnel at the Aerospace Laboratory for Lasers, ElectroMagnetics, and Optics of Texas A&M University, tailored for optical diagnostic development and sub-scale fundamental compressible fluid dynamics research. A Ludwieg tube tunnel architecture was selected due to its robustness, versatility, and low operational costs. The tunnel consists of a 50-foot-long driver tube constructed from modular Tri-Clamp spools, a Mach 4 nozzle with 3 in. exit diameter configured as a free jet, and a fast-acting valve with 14 ms opening time for high-duty-cycle operation. Such construction proved to be a robust, compact, and affordable solution for academic applications. Characterization methods consisted of simultaneous high-speed dot-schlieren, total and static pressure measurements, and femtosecond laser electronic excitation tagging. Average flow velocity for the first steady-state test time was measured via FLEET at (668.0 ± 5.7) m/s. recent_works.title: 3D Nitric Oxide Imaging by Laser-Induced Fluorescence in a Reacting Flow Using Tunable 5th Harmonic Burst-Mode Nd:YAG
recent_works.abstract: We present burst-mode, volumetric laser-induced fluorescence measurements of nitric oxide in a quasi-"frozen" reacting flow with laser excitation via the 5th harmonic of a Nd:YAG laser. A tunable pulse-burst laser generated 5th harmonic radiation near 212.9 nm at 200 kHz with pulse energies of 5 mJ/pulse. The UV output beam was formed into a 55-mm tall sheet and swept across a 25-mm distance within a turbulent oxy-acetylene torch plume. The laser was tuned to overlap the gamma(1, 0) Q2 (43) transition of nitric oxide at 212.885 nm (vac.), which was formed naturally within the reacting plume. The set of PLIF images captured by a high-speed camera during the laser sweep were stacked to yield 3D renderings of the distribution of nitric oxide within the flow. The close spacing of the laser sheets led to high resolution 3D renderings with a voxel size of as small as 220 × 220 × 115 micrometers.
